\begin{abstract}
Scam messages reach users through several channels, yet the machine-learning
filters that intercept them usually return a verdict without a reason. We
present an interpretable multi-modal framework that detects fraudulent SMS and
e-mail messages and explains every decision. Each channel has a specialist
pipeline that maps URLs, phone numbers and money amounts to readable
placeholder tokens, combines TF--IDF features with fifteen stylometric
statistics, and fuses Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost by
F1-weighted soft voting; LIME explains the full ensemble and exact TreeSHAP the
boosted component. On held-out splits of the UCI SMS Spam Collection and the
Enron-Spam corpus, the ensemble reaches 98.55\% accuracy (ROC-AUC 0.9941) on
SMS and 98.25\% (ROC-AUC 0.9983) on e-mail. Paired McNemar and DeLong tests show
that it significantly outperforms both tree learners on e-mail ($p\le0.003$)
and ties Logistic Regression, and a word-deletion test confirms that LIME's
explanations are faithful. Global attributions show that stylometric features
dominate SMS decisions and expose a corpus shortcut: the token \tok{enron}
occurs in 42\% of legitimate test e-mails and in no spam, and appending it to
spam e-mails flips 35.5\% of the ensemble's detections (91.7\% for XGBoost
alone).
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Spam detection, smishing, phishing, explainable artificial intelligence, SHAP,
LIME, ensemble learning, shortcut learning, stylometry.
\end{IEEEkeywords}

%==============================================================================
\section{Introduction}
%==============================================================================

Fraudulent messaging is the most frequently reported form of cybercrime: in
2025 the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center logged more than one million
complaints and US\$20.9 billion in losses, with phishing and spoofing again the
largest category (191,561 complaints)~\cite{fbi2026ic3}. Large language models
(LLMs) now let attackers write persuasive, personalised phishing at negligible
cost~\cite{heiding2024devising,yao2024survey}, and scams have followed banking
and one-time-password traffic onto SMS~\cite{mehmood2024smishing}.

Machine-learning filters intercept most of this traffic, but they are usually
black boxes: a message is blocked and nobody can say why. High accuracy can
hide shortcuts, spurious cues that happen to separate the classes in one
dataset~\cite{du2024shortcut}, and although explainable AI (XAI) now offers a
broad toolkit~\cite{longo2024xai}, explanations in spam filtering are mostly
shown as illustrations rather than tested for faithfulness~\cite{lyu2024faithful}
or used to audit the model. Most detectors also serve a single channel,
although SMS and e-mail differ sharply (a median of 12 versus 155 words and
12\% versus 48\% spam in the corpora used here), and comparisons on
near-saturated benchmarks rarely report uncertainty.

We address these gaps with an interpretable multi-modal framework, where
\emph{modality} denotes the messaging channel (SMS or e-mail). Our
contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item a CPU-only pipeline with one specialist per channel: readable
        placeholder tokens, TF--IDF plus fifteen named stylometric features,
        and Logistic Regression (LR), Random Forest (RF) and XGBoost (XGB)
        fused by F1-weighted soft voting;
  \item a statistically grounded evaluation with bootstrap confidence
        intervals, McNemar and DeLong tests, and an end-to-end evaluation of
        channel routing and cross-channel transfer;
  \item a dual explanation layer (LIME for the full ensemble, exact TreeSHAP
        for XGBoost) whose faithfulness is tested by word deletion; and
  \item an explanation-driven audit that uncovers and quantifies a corpus
        shortcut, and a sparse-versus-dense pitfall that silently invalidates
        SHAP explanations of XGBoost text models.
\end{enumerate}

%==============================================================================
\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}
%==============================================================================

\emph{SMS spam and smishing.} Reproducible SMS research rests on the UCI SMS
Spam Collection~\cite{almeida2011sms}. Recent detectors are mostly deep or
transformer models, such as a smishing detector designed to reduce false
positives~\cite{mehmood2024smishing} and a transformer detector with an
explainability analysis~\cite{uddin2025explainabledetector}; Hur \emph{et al.}
found LLMs robust and effective for SMS spam~\cite{hur2026llm}. \c{S}ahin
\emph{et al.} benchmarked classical learners across text representations on
the same corpus and found the representation more decisive than classifier
complexity~\cite{sahin2026revisiting}. Work on other languages such as Swahili
is growing~\cite{mambina2024swahili}, and Salman \emph{et al.} released a new
dataset and analysed spammers' evasive techniques~\cite{salman2024evasive}.

\emph{E-mail spam and phishing.} The Enron-Spam corpus~\cite{metsis2006spam}
remains a standard e-mail benchmark. Fine-tuned transformers and LLMs dominate
recent work~\cite{jamal2024improved,roumeliotis2024next,uddin2026explainable,koide2026chatspamdetector};
Mel\'{e}ndez \emph{et al.} found transformers ahead of traditional models for
phishing e-mail, by a small margin~\cite{melendez2024comparative}, and
meta-learner ensembles remain competitive~\cite{kshirsagar2025metalearner}.
Hadi \emph{et al.} target both channels with a deep--shallow
hybrid~\cite{hadi2026hybrid}. LLMs can author effective phishing at
scale~\cite{heiding2024devising}, and Opara \emph{et al.} showed that such
messages can bypass major webmail filters but are detectable with stylometric
features~\cite{opara2025evaluating}.

\emph{Explainability and shortcuts.} LIME fits a local surrogate around one
prediction~\cite{ribeiro2016lime}; SHAP assigns additive Shapley
attributions~\cite{lundberg2017shap}, computed exactly for trees by
TreeSHAP~\cite{lundberg2020treeshap}. Explanations have accompanied smishing
detectors~\cite{prince2026explainable,jasim2026fuzzy}, guided feature
selection for spam~\cite{shambour2025quantum}, and been compared on boosting
models, where SHAP was more stable globally than LIME~\cite{panthi2026shaplime}.
They are not trustworthy by default: faithfulness must be
measured~\cite{lyu2024faithful}, explainers often disagree~\cite{krishna2024disagreement},
and many challenges remain open~\cite{longo2024xai}. Shortcut learning, the
exploitation of spurious dataset cues, is well documented in
NLP~\cite{du2024shortcut,dogra2024shortcut}; spam corpora are vulnerable
because legitimate mail often comes from a single organisation.

Table~\ref{tab:related} contrasts representative recent studies. Most address
one channel and use explanations mainly as illustrations. We combine two
channel specialists with a dual explanation layer, test its faithfulness, use
it to audit the model, and compare learners with paired significance tests.

\section{Proposed Framework}\label{sec:method}
%==============================================================================

Fig.~\ref{fig:arch} shows the architecture. A message is routed to the
specialist of its channel; each specialist has its own normalisation, feature
space and ensemble, and returns a label, a spam probability and explanations.

\subsection{Normalisation and Features}

Text is lower-cased, HTML tags are stripped, and high-signal entities are
\emph{mapped} rather than deleted: URLs become \tok{httpaddr}, e-mail addresses
\tok{emailaddr}, currency amounts \tok{moneysymb}, phone numbers
\tok{phonenumbr} and other numbers \tok{numbr}. These are among the strongest
scam signals, and as readable tokens they can appear in an explanation; no
stemming is applied, so every explained token is a recognisable word. The text
is vectorised with sublinear TF--IDF over uni- and bi-grams (3,000 terms with
$\mathrm{df}\ge2$ for SMS, 5,000 with $\mathrm{df}\ge3$ for e-mail). Fifteen
stylometric statistics computed on the \emph{raw} message
(Table~\ref{tab:features}) are scaled by their training maximum and appended,
giving 3,015 and 5,015 dimensions; their upper-case names keep them distinct
from vocabulary in every explanation.

\begin{table}[!t]
\caption{Engineered Stylometric Features (Computed on the Raw Message)}
\label{tab:features}
\centering
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{3.05cm}L{4.7cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Feature} & \textbf{Description} \\
\midrule
\tok{CHAR_COUNT}, \tok{WORD_COUNT} & Length in characters / words \\
\tok{AVG_WORD_LEN} & Mean word length \\
\tok{DIGIT_RATIO} & Share of characters that are digits \\
\tok{UPPERCASE_RATIO} & Share of letters in upper case \\
\tok{ALLCAPS_WORDS} & Words written fully in capitals \\
\tok{PUNCT_RATIO} & Share of punctuation characters \\
\tok{SPECIAL_CHAR_RATIO} & Share of non-alphanumeric characters \\
\tok{NUM_EXCLAMATIONS} & Count of ``!'' \\
\tok{NUM_QUESTIONS} & Count of ``?'' \\
\tok{NUM_CURRENCY} & Currency symbols and money amounts \\
\tok{NUM_URLS}, \tok{NUM_EMAILS} & Detected links / e-mail addresses \\
\tok{NUM_PHONES} & Detected phone numbers \\
\tok{SPAM_KEYWORDS} & Hits in a 46-word, human-auditable scam lexicon \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsection{Base Learners and Weighted Soft Voting}

Three learners with different inductive biases provide diversity: LR
(liblinear, $C=1$) and RF~\cite{breiman2001random} (250 trees, minimum leaf
size 2) with balanced class weights, and XGBoost~\cite{chen2016xgboost} (300
trees, depth 6, learning rate 0.1, subsampling 0.9/0.8) with
$\mathrm{scale\_pos\_weight}=N_{\text{ham}}/N_{\text{spam}}$. Re-weighting was
preferred to synthetic oversampling so that every training example remains a
real, explainable message. The ensemble averages the learners' probabilities,
\begin{equation}
  p(\text{spam}\mid x)=\sum_{m=1}^{3} w_m\,p_m(\text{spam}\mid x),
  \label{eq:ensemble}
\end{equation}
with $w_m$ proportional to each learner's mean F1 in stratified 5-fold
cross-validation on the training split, and predicts spam when $p\ge0.5$. The
weights are 0.3329/0.3331/0.3340 (LR/RF/XGB) for SMS and 0.3356/0.3311/0.3333
for e-mail, so any benefit comes from diversity rather than from a dominant
member.

\subsection{Channel Router}

A transparent rule selects the specialist: a message is treated as e-mail if
it exceeds 280 characters, contains a line break or contains a cue word
(\emph{subject}, \emph{dear}, \emph{regards}, \emph{sincerely},
\emph{unsubscribe}, \emph{attached}), and as SMS otherwise. Users can override
the choice in the application.

\subsection{Explanation Layer}

LIME~\cite{ribeiro2016lime} removes words from the raw message, re-scores
1,000 perturbations through the \emph{entire} pipeline and fits a local linear
surrogate, so it explains the complete ensemble through its ten most
influential words. For XGBoost, SHAP values decompose the log-odds output
additively, $f(x)=\phi_0+\sum_j\phi_j(x)$~\cite{lundberg2017shap}, and are
computed exactly by TreeSHAP~\cite{lundberg2020treeshap}; global importance is
the mean $|\phi_j|$ over 800 held-out messages. One implementation detail is
critical: XGBoost treats entries absent from a sparse matrix as
\emph{missing}, whereas a densified copy turns them into zeros that follow
different branches. Densifying the input before explaining therefore explains
a different function: it changes the XGBoost verdict for 729 of 1,032 SMS and
1,182 of 2,400 e-mail test messages. All attributions here use XGBoost's
native TreeSHAP on the sparse matrix the model actually scores.

%==============================================================================
\section{Experimental Setup}\label{sec:setup}
%==============================================================================

The UCI SMS Spam Collection~\cite{almeida2011sms} is used in full, and a
class-stratified sample of 12,000 messages (subject and body) is drawn from the
Enron-Spam corpus~\cite{metsis2006spam}, after removing empty and duplicate
messages (Table~\ref{tab:data}). Each corpus is split 80/20 with
stratification (seed 42); all fitting, including the cross-validated ensemble
weights, uses the training split only, and the test split is used once. We
report accuracy, precision, recall, F1, MCC, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC and the Brier
score, with 95\% bootstrap confidence intervals (2,000 resamples). The
ensemble is compared with each base learner on the same messages using the
exact McNemar test~\cite{mcnemar1947note} and DeLong's test for correlated ROC
curves~\cite{delong1988comparing}, Holm-corrected within each channel.

\begin{table}[!t]
\caption{Corpora After Cleaning and De-duplication}
\label{tab:data}
\centering
\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Channel} & \textbf{Messages} & \textbf{Spam} & \textbf{Median words} & \textbf{Train} & \textbf{Test} \\
\midrule
SMS~\cite{almeida2011sms} & 5,158 & 642 (12.4\%) & 12 & 4,126 & 1,032 \\
E-mail~\cite{metsis2006spam} & 12,000 & 5,792 (48.3\%) & 155 & 9,600 & 2,400 \\
\bottomrule

We further evaluate (i) the router on the pooled test sets (3,432 messages)
and each specialist on the other channel; (ii) LIME faithfulness, by deleting
the top-$k$ LIME words ($k\in\{1,3,5\}$) from 60 SMS and 25 e-mail correctly
detected spam messages and comparing the drop in spam probability with that
from deleting $k$ random words; and (iii) the shortcut surfaced by the global
attributions, by deleting the token from legitimate test e-mails and
inserting it into spam. The framework is implemented in Python with
scikit-learn, XGBoost, SHAP and LIME and served through a four-tab Streamlit
application; a 13-check smoke test covers the whole pipeline, and re-running
training reproduces all metrics exactly. Timings use a 10-core ARM64 CPU
without a GPU.

\subsection{Classification Performance and Significance}

Table~\ref{tab:results} and Fig.~\ref{fig:roc} report all four systems. On SMS
the ensemble reaches 98.55\% accuracy with the highest precision (0.9669),
only 4 false positives among 904 legitimate messages and the best PR-AUC and
Brier score; on e-mail it reaches 98.25\% with the highest recall (0.9940; 7 of
1,158 spam messages missed) and ROC-AUC (0.9983). The SMS specialist favours
precision, which suits a channel where a blocked message may be a one-time
password; the e-mail specialist favours recall. LR is a strong baseline: it
matches the ensemble's SMS accuracy and slightly exceeds its SMS F1 and e-mail
accuracy.

The paired tests (Table~\ref{tab:significance}) resolve these small
differences. On SMS none is significant. On e-mail the ensemble beats both
tree models (McNemar: 24 vs.\ 5 discordant messages against RF and 22 vs.\ 4
against XGB, $p=0.002$; DeLong $p\le0.003$) but is statistically
indistinguishable from LR (11 vs.\ 13, $p=0.84$).

\subsection{Routing and Cross-Channel Transfer}\label{sec:routing}

The specialists do not transfer (Table~\ref{tab:routing}): the SMS model is at
chance on e-mail (ROC-AUC 0.53), and the e-mail model flags 88\% of legitimate
SMS as spam. The router sends 96.4\% of SMS and 85.1\% of e-mails to the right
specialist, but misrouted e-mails (short, without cue words) are classified
correctly only 42.3\% of the time, so pooled accuracy falls from 98.34\% with
oracle routing to 92.16\% with automatic routing. The heuristic router, not
the classifiers, is the weakest component, hence the manual override.

\subsection{Local and Global Explanations}

Fig.~\ref{fig:local} explains an illustrative smishing SMS written by the
authors and absent from both corpora: ``URGENT! You have WON a \pounds 2,000
cash prize GUARANTEED. Call 09061701461 now or visit www.claim-your-prize.com
to claim!'' All learners vote spam (ensemble 0.996). LIME ranks the
premium-rate number highest, followed by the money amount and scam vocabulary;
TreeSHAP attributes the decision mainly to stylometry (digit ratio, word
length, lexicon hits, capitals) and the \tok{httpaddr} and \tok{phonenumbr}
placeholders. LIME speaks in the user's words, SHAP in the model's features.

Globally (Fig.~\ref{fig:global}), eight of the ten most important SMS features
are stylometric, and the fifteen engineered features (0.5\% of the dimensions)
carry 74.5\% of the attribution mass: a short scam is betrayed by its
\emph{shape} as much as by its words. On e-mail a single word, \tok{enron},
dominates with about three times the attribution of the next feature.

\begin{figure}[!t]
\centering

\subsection{Faithfulness of the Local Explanations}

On SMS, deleting the top LIME word lowers the ensemble's spam probability 8.6
times more than deleting a random word (Table~\ref{tab:lime}); deleting the
top five lowers it by 0.455 and flips 52\% of the verdicts. E-mail drops are
smaller in absolute terms, because long messages contain redundant evidence,
but about 20 times larger than random. LIME therefore points at words on
which the decision genuinely depends.

\subsection{Explanations as an Audit Tool: A Corpus Shortcut}

The token \tok{enron} occurs in 44.4\% of legitimate training and 42.1\% of
legitimate test e-mails but in \emph{no} spam: every legitimate message is
internal Enron correspondence, so the company name is a one-sided proxy for
ham. Its mean TreeSHAP contribution is $-3.95$ log-odds when present versus
$+0.66$ when absent; other identity cues such as the first name \emph{vince}
also rank highly, and none of the ensemble's 35 false positives contains the
token. Table~\ref{tab:shortcut} quantifies the risk. Deleting the token from
523 legitimate e-mails flips only 11 verdicts, but \emph{appending} the single
word to spam flips 409 of 1,151 detections (35.5\%). XGBoost alone is evaded on
91.7\% of messages, RF on 25.3\% and LR on 4.5\%, so the heterogeneous ensemble
is far more robust than its boosted member, yet not immune. The shortcut is
invisible in Tables~\ref{tab:results} and~\ref{tab:significance}; only the
explanations revealed it.

\subsection{Computational Cost}

Training both specialists, including cross-validation, takes about 1.5 minutes
on a CPU (Table~\ref{tab:cost}). A verdict takes about 15\,ms, a TreeSHAP
attribution under 1\,ms and a LIME explanation 0.08--0.21\,s, so every
prediction can be explained interactively.

%==============================================================================
\section{Discussion and Limitations}\label{sec:discussion}
%==============================================================================

All learners exceed 97\% accuracy, and a regularised linear model on
well-designed features is as accurate as the ensemble, consistent with the
finding that representation matters more than classifier complexity for SMS
spam~\cite{sahin2026revisiting}. The ensemble's value lies in better ranking
metrics, a precision-first SMS profile, significant gains over both tree
models on e-mail and, above all, robustness to the shortcut attack. The
\tok{enron} shortcut is a property of the corpus rather than the pipeline, yet
a black-box deployment would have shipped it silently. Global explanations are
therefore an auditing instrument, but they must themselves be
validated~\cite{lyu2024faithful}: the sparse/dense pitfall yields plausible
SHAP plots of a function the deployed model never computes. We recommend
computing tree attributions on the exact input the model scores, validating
explanations by deletion, screening global attributions for corpus
identifiers, and evaluating routing as well as classification.

The corpora are English and date from 2000--2012, so modern and code-mixed
smishing and LLM-generated phishing~\cite{opara2025evaluating} are not
covered, and the shortcut means e-mail accuracy overstates performance on
other organisations' mail. Results come from one stratified split, the router
is heuristic, SHAP covers only the boosted component, and neither transformer
or LLM detectors nor adversarial obfuscation~\cite{salman2024evasive} were
evaluated.

%==============================================================================
\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
%==============================================================================

We presented an interpretable multi-modal framework that detects scam SMS and
e-mail with channel-specific ensembles of LR, RF and XGBoost and explains every
verdict with LIME and exact TreeSHAP. It reaches 98.55\% (SMS) and 98.25\%
(e-mail) accuracy, significantly outperforms both tree learners on e-mail and
trains in minutes on a CPU. Its explanations are faithful, show that
stylometry rivals vocabulary on SMS, and exposed a corpus shortcut that a
one-word insertion can exploit. Future work will test cross-corpus
generalisation and remove identity shortcuts, extend the framework to
multilingual and code-mixed data including Indian languages, learn the
router, and benchmark transformer and LLM detectors under the same protocol.
